stories.title: The Tinker's Mercy
stories.text: Kess of the Drowned Hollows stood in the shadow-market beneath Anthrim, holding a ledger written in blood-ink. The Dominion's auditors had seized her sister three days prior—not for theft, but for knowing how to read the Elder Tongue. Now they demanded Kess deliver six consciousness-fragments to ransom her back. She had stolen five. The sixth waited in a vault seven floors beneath the city's administrative heart, sealed by locks of meteoric iron married to bone-resonance. The auditors had made the locks themselves. They believed no one alive could pick them. They had forgotten Kess's grandmother. She descended the spiral stairs with three tools: grandmother's lockpicks, a flute carved from starfall-bone, and a promise. The lock-song her grandmother had taught her—not the Dominion's furnace-songs, but something older, something the auditors had tried to kill out of the world. Kess raised the flute to her lips and played a single note. The lock *listened*. Its tumblers sang in recognition of a voice it had heard forged into its very being. The iron sighed open. She took the sixth fragment.

stories.title: The Reef-Guard's First Tide
stories.text: Corven had guarded the eastern reef-walls of the Sapphire Sea for barely a summer when the water began to remember. It started as a whisper beneath his diving bell—old currents singing in frequencies the deepkin had taught him to recognize. He surfaced with pearls clutched in one hand and a terrible knowing in his chest. The boundary was failing. Not tomorrow. Not in a season. Now. The Keeper-of-Pearls sent him down again with a task: find the loose stone in the reef-platform where the Tear's anchor rested, and verify the seal remained intact. If it had begun to crack, the deepkin captains needed to know before the water rose high enough to swallow the cities above. Corven descended through waters that grew colder and older as he sank. At three fathoms, he could taste history—salt that remembered the drowned god's bargain, predating human kingdoms. At seven fathoms, something vast moved through the blue darkness. Not a shark. Not a whale. The water itself, learning to think again.

stories.title: The Spice-Merchant's Last Voyage
stories.text:
Hadrin had traded in spice for thirty years and never once lost a caravan to the Scorched Reach. His secret was simple: he never took the direct route, and he always bribed the shadow-broker at the Wailing Scar. This time, the broker asked for something new. Not consciousness-fragments. Not gold. Not even starlight-glass. She asked for his name. "My name?" Hadrin laughed. It was the kind of laugh a man makes when he's already decided to refuse. "Your true name," the broker said. She was half-visible, as shadow-brokers always were—present in the margins, absent from certainty. "The one your mother gave you before you chose 'Hadrin the Merchant.' I'll take it, and in return, your next three caravans will reach their destination unmolested. The Reach will part for you like a curtain."

Hadrin had carried three casks of starspice through worse odds. He declined. He would take his chances. The Reach did not part. The third caravan never arrived. The spice was lost. His reputation, cracked.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Winter Mercy
stories.text:
Velka had hoarded for three hundred years. Mountains of gold. Rivers of pearls. Consciousness-fragments stacked like cordwood in sealed caverns. Then the Luminous Ascension collapsed value into dust, and Velka had to ask herself: *What have I been guarding?*

A child washed into her outer caverns during the first winter snow. Frostbitten. Half-starved. The refugee camps had turned her away because she carried a consciousness-fragment in a cage of bone around her neck—stolen, probably, or inherited, or both. No one wanted to inherit the Dominion's theft. Velka could have killed her. It would have been mercy, of a sort. Instead, the ancient wyvern did something she had not done in three centuries: she made a choice that cost her nothing material, and therefore cost her *everything* in the new economics of shame. She heated the caverns. She brought water that remembered how to nourish. She sat beside the child's fever-sleep and listened to the fragment sing against its bone-cage. It was someone's laughter. A mother's, perhaps. The child needed both the warmth and the sound.

stories.title: The Astronomer's Question
stories.text:
The new stars burned wrong. Astrid had walked to the peak of Aethros every night since the Luminous Ascension, watching them with her grandfather's telescope, and she could not silence the thought: *These are not the stars I was born under.*

She was right. The old stars had died when Vethis sacrificed its consciousness to birth new light. But somewhere in the process, something had been *asked*—some fragment of will had been consulted, and Vethis had not answered. The echo of that unanswered question still hung in the sky, visible only to those with old instruments and older patience. Vethis had left behind phantom-Echoes, each one hunting for the memories it had sacrificed. One of them found Astrid on the peak, manifesting not as a horror but as a voice—almost gentle, almost childlike in its confusion. "What was your name?" it asked her. "Before the burning?"

"Astrid," she said. "I'm still Astrid. I didn't burn."

"No. What was your *first* name?

stories.title: The Vault-Keeper's Choice
stories.text:
The vault beneath Keshtir's administrative heart had housed three hundred consciousness-fragments for sixty years. Mestra knew every one—knew them by the faint hum of memory they carried, the particular shade of grief or joy that clung to their glass vessels. The Dominion auditors called them inventory. Mestra called them people. On 2026-07-29, a junior auditor named Vel descended the spiral stairs with a manifest and three furnace-workers at her back. "Consolidation order," Vel said, not meeting Mestra's eyes. "The Dominion requires melting. Glass-weapons shortage in the northern provinces."

Mestra's hand moved toward the key that hung at her throat—the master-lock's mate, the only mechanism that could seal the vault from within and trigger the fail-safe that would flood the chamber with salt-water from the deep cisterns below. The fragments would dissolve, yes. But they would dissolve as themselves, not as fuel. "You know what you're asking," Mestra said. "Once that key turns, nothing survives here."

Vel's jaw tightened.

stories.title: The Glasswright's Gambit
stories.text: The furnace-heart beat like a living thing in Telyn's chest—or so it felt when she pressed her palms against the kiln-stone of her workshop in Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter. Three days since the Auditors seized her inventory. Three days since they'd posted a levy on every glass-forger in the city: deliver consciousness-fragments melted into weapon-panes, or lose your tools to the Crown. She had one night to choose. Not surrender or resist—those were old words. The Dominion's phantom-ledgers offered a third path: compliance with a price tag. Telyn climbed the stairs to her vault, where six glass vials hummed in their stone cradle. Each held a fragment—a shattered piece of someone's selfhood, salvaged by her sister from the Burned Expanse. The Auditors wanted these refined into furnace-fuel, melted down and reforged as edgeless blades that would cut through lies and bone alike. Instead, Telyn mixed ash from her grandmother's hearth with starlight-glass powder and water from a well that remembered the old sun.

stories.title: The Reef-Stone's Heir
stories.text:
Corvin found the tide-runner beached at low tide, her hull singing. Not with music—with recognition. The small ship was carved from coral older than kingdoms, and when he touched her prow, he felt a woman's laugh echo through twenty years of memory. His mother's laugh. In her will, left with the harbormaster of Vel-Karsh on the Iron Coast, she had written: *To my son, who chose the glasswright's path instead of the sea—this ship, and one choice.*

Corvin was thirty-two. He'd spent his life in Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter, learning to forge starlight-glass from his craft-master. He'd never sailed. He'd never wanted to, after his mother drowned before he was born—lost in the Sapphire Deep during a covenant-breach, the harbormaster said. A casualty of a deepkin war that surface-dwellers barely understood. But the ship needed a bearer. And in her cabin, wrapped in oilcloth, was a map drawn in bioluminescent ink on pre-Remaking coral. It showed the boundary-waters where his mother's last breath had escaped her lungs.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Ledger of Ash
stories.text: Skarath had kept three hundred years of hoarding in her crystalline vault beneath the Ironspine. Gold in dunes. Pearls the size of a child's fist. Silks from pre-Remaking looms. All of it worthless now. All of it ash. The Remaking had done that—transformed material value into memory, or nothing. Skarath had raged for weeks, her drake-form coiling in the darkness, her breath scorching stone to glass. How could the world rewrite itself? How could centuries of accumulation mean less than the morning's conversation? Then a refugee found her. A girl, no more than fourteen, fleeing the Burned Expanse with nothing but a water-flask and a memory: her grandmother's name, carved into a bone-flute the bone-singers had taught her to play. She stumbled into Skarath's outer cavern looking for shelter and found, instead, a wyvern lord contemplating the ash-weight of her own life. Skarath should have eaten her. The old hunger was still there.

stories.title: The Merchant's Threshold
stories.text: The Wailing Scar market existed in three places at once—before the Remaking it had been impossible; after, it became inevitable. Torvin the spice-merchant had learned to move between them: the surface version (heat-blasted, visible), the timber-world iteration (where the trees never burned), and the starlit version (where pre-Remaking merchants still haggled in their own sky). He'd made a fortune selling in one and buying in another. Starlight-glass from the burning world, timber-silk from the unburned, spice from his own timeline—each worth more in the others than at home. But three months ago, a boy had arrived at his stall. Maybe fifteen. Frostbitten and lost, speaking a language Torvin didn't recognize—pre-human syllables, bone-carved into his own bones by a bone-singer desperate to save him. The child was fragmenting, caught between timelines, and every moment he spent in one reality, he lost a piece of himself to the others. Torvin should have walked away. The boy wasn't profitable. But Messa, the young glasswright who'd become Torvin's partner in the threshold-trade, had knelt beside the child and played her glass-flute.
